title: How to change the color mode in Photoshop on Mac: step-by-step for RGB and CMYK
metaTitle: How to Change the Color Mode in Photoshop on Mac
description: Learn how to change the color mode in Photoshop on Mac: pick RGB or CMYK from Image > Mode, save a copy first, and fix greyed-out menus.
targetKeyword: how to change the color mode in photoshop on mac
intro: To change the color mode in Photoshop on Mac, open the file, go to Image > Mode, and pick RGB Color for screens or CMYK Color for print. Photoshop may warn that converting will flatten layers, discard channels, or reduce color information, so save a copy of the file first.
tldr: Go to Image > Mode and choose RGB Color for screens or CMYK Color for commercial print.
Save a copy before you convert. The warning can mention flattened layers, discarded channels, or reduced color.
Bitmap only becomes available after you convert the file to Grayscale first.
If Mode is greyed out or CMYK is missing, check for 32 Bits/Channel or an active Quick Mask.

blocks.text: What the color mode controls

A color mode tells Photoshop how to describe the colors in your file. RGB builds color from red, green, and blue light, which is how your Mac screen shows images. CMYK describes color with cyan, magenta, yellow, and black ink, which is how most commercial printers work. Grayscale keeps only brightness, with no color at all. Bitmap is pure black and white, with no shades of gray in between.

The mode you pick decides what the file can do next. A design built in RGB and sent to a press may print duller than it looked on screen. Inks cover a different range of colors than a display does. Converting back from CMYK to RGB does not restore colors that were lost along the way, so keep an RGB master whenever you can.
Check the current mode before you change it

Open the file and go to Image > Mode. The mode you are in is the one marked in that submenu. Look before you change anything. That tells you whether you are converting to something new or only confirming the setting. If you use Photoshop on the web, the options are narrower, as the web section below explains.
Step by step: change the color mode in Photoshop on Mac

The steps below follow one path. Go to Image > Mode, pick the mode you need, then deal with the warning. Before any of that, save a copy. The slow part is usually checking colors afterward, not the menu itself.
Pick the right color mode for your job

items: RGB Color: screens, the web, video, and most on-screen design work.
CMYK Color: commercial print. Ask your printer whether they want a specific profile.
Grayscale: black-and-white photos and single-ink output. It removes color from the image.
Bitmap: pure black and white with no grays. It only works after the file is in Grayscale.

blocks.text: Bitmap trips up more people than any other mode. Photoshop does not let you go straight from RGB to Bitmap. Convert to Grayscale first, then choose Bitmap from the same Mode submenu. Expert Photography describes the same two-step order.
Read the warning before you click OK

When you convert, Photoshop may show a warning. The warning says converting will flatten layers, discard channels, or reduce color information. Read it before you click through. Flattening merges all layers into one. Discarded channels, such as alpha or spot channels, can disappear from the file. Reduced color means some shades get merged into the nearest value the new mode can hold.

blocks.title: Save a copy first
blocks.text: Use File > Save As before you convert. Keep the RGB original with its layers, so you can make a new CMYK file later without starting over.
Fix a greyed-out Mode menu or missing CMYK

Greyed-out options usually come from one of two causes. The first is bit depth. A file at 32 Bits/Channel can block CMYK and other modes. Go to Image > Mode, choose 8 Bits/Channel, then try again. The second is Quick Mask. While Quick Mask is on, Photoshop limits what you can change. Press Q to turn it off, or delete the Quick Mask channel. Adobe Community threads from 2015 to 2024 describe both causes, and the menus may look a little different on your version.

blocks.text: Colors can shift after converting on macOS

Some Mac users see black artifacts or banding during RGB-to-CMYK conversion. Omnimend reports this in Photoshop 27.8 and later on macOS Tahoe when the GPU is enabled. The workaround it describes is to turn off Use Graphics Processor under Photoshop > Settings > Performance, then convert again. Check your version first.

A separate bug affected Photoshop 27.9.0 on Mac. The main canvas could look washed out while the same image looked normal elsewhere. Adobe says the fix arrived in 27.9.1, so update if you see that problem.
Photoshop on the web and CMYK work

If you use Photoshop on the web, check the mode before you start. A third-party article from March 2026 says the web version works in RGB only. It says CMYK print work must stay on desktop. The same article says the web version defaults to sRGB. Adobe's product page does not discuss color modes, so treat these limits as reported, not official.

The same article reports that files above roughly 100 to 200 MB can lag or fail, and that the browser slows down above 15 to 20 layers. It does not explain how it tested those limits. Use the numbers as rough guides, and keep large print files on desktop.
Which Photoshop version this applies to

The Image > Mode path is the same in the desktop releases covered by these sources. CGChannel covered Photoshop 27.6 in April 2026 and Photoshop 27.11 in September 2026. Both list macOS 14.0 or later as the minimum. Neither release coverage mentions a color mode or Mode menu change. Adobe's full release notes were not available for this check, so confirm the Mode menu on your own version.
A worked example: a flyer for print

Say you built a flyer for screen preview, and the printer now asks for a CMYK file. Start with File > Save As and name the copy flyer-print. On that copy, go to Image > Mode > CMYK Color and read the warning. Click through once you know what it will change.

Then compare the copy with the RGB original. Check the reds, the blues, and any logo color. If something is off, adjust in RGB and convert again. Keeping the RGB master untouched makes that loop quick, and it costs you nothing to keep it.
Common mistakes to avoid

items: Converting the only copy. Save As first, then convert the copy, not the original.
Converting a screen file to CMYK for no reason. Screens gain nothing, and you lose some color range.
Ignoring the warning. Flattened layers are hard to get back once the file is overwritten.
Trusting the screen alone for print colors. Ask the printer for a proof before a large run.

blocks.text: Check the result and what comes next

After you convert, open Image > Mode and confirm the mode is set. Look at the parts of the image where color matters most, such as skin tones and brand colors. If anything looks wrong, press ⌘Z to undo and try a different approach.

Resize and crop first, then convert last. That order keeps your edits in the color space you designed in. Converting first and cropping afterward means you edit in a mode you did not plan to use. Related guides: [resize an image in Photoshop](/how-to/resize-an-image-in-photoshop), [crop an image in Photoshop](/how-to/crop-an-image-in-photoshop), and [fix PSD files that won't open](/how-to/fix-psd-files-that-won-t-open-in-photoshop). If the menus look different after an update, [check your Photoshop version](/how-to/check-your-photoshop-version-in-photoshop) first.

faq.question: Will changing the color mode delete my layers?
faq.answer: It can. Photoshop may warn that converting will flatten layers, so read the dialog before you click OK. Save a copy first, and keep the original PSD with its layers as your master file.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for Image > Mode on Mac?
faq.answer: The Mac shortcut list I checked did not include one for Image > Mode, so use the menu. Search results point to ⇧⌘K for Color Settings, but that was not confirmed on an official page. Check the Edit menu for Color Settings before you rely on that shortcut.

faq.question: Why is CMYK greyed out on my Mac?
faq.answer: Usually the file is at 32 Bits/Channel, or Quick Mask is on. Switch to 8 Bits/Channel under Image > Mode, and turn off Quick Mask with Q. Adobe Community threads from 2015 to 2024 describe these same causes.

faq.question: Can I change the color mode in Photoshop on the web?
faq.answer: A third-party article says the web version works in RGB only, and that CMYK print work stays on desktop. Adobe's product page does not discuss color modes. Confirm in the app before you plan a print job.

faq.question: Which Photoshop version does this page cover?
faq.answer: The Image > Mode path is the same in the desktop releases covered by these sources. Those are 27.6 from April 2026 and 27.11 from September 2026, and both list macOS 14.0 or later. Adobe's full release notes did not load, so confirm the menu on your version.

faq.question: Do colors change when I convert to CMYK?
faq.answer: Yes, colors can shift because CMYK covers a different range of colors than RGB. Check skin tones, logos, and brand colors after you convert. On macOS Tahoe with the GPU on, Photoshop 27.8 and later can show black artifacts, so try turning off Use Graphics Processor.

faq.question: Can I go back to RGB after converting to CMYK?
faq.answer: Yes, with Image > Mode > RGB Color. The colors do not return to their original values, though. Keep the RGB master so you never need to reverse a conversion.

task: Change the color mode of a file in Photoshop on Mac
appliesTo: Photoshop 27.6 and 27.11 on macOS 14.0 or later, desktop app
requirements: Photoshop desktop app on macOS 14.0 or later, per CGChannel's 27.6 and 27.11 coverage
A file you can save a copy of, such as a PSD with layers
An open document, because the Mode menu needs a file loaded

steps.name: Open the file and check the current mode
steps.text: Open the file in Photoshop, then go to Image > Mode. The mode in use is the one marked in that submenu. Note it before you change anything, so you know what you are converting from.

steps.name: Save a copy before you convert
steps.text: Go to File > Save As and name the copy. Converting can flatten layers and discard channels, so keep the original untouched.
steps.tip: Name the copy so you can tell it apart, such as flyer-print.psd.

steps.name: Open the Mode submenu
steps.text: Go to Image > Mode. The list includes Bitmap, Grayscale, Duotone, RGB Color, and CMYK Color, along with the bit-depth options.

steps.name: Choose RGB Color or CMYK Color
steps.text: Click RGB Color for screen, web, and video work. Click CMYK Color for commercial print, and ask your printer whether they want a specific profile.

steps.name: Convert to Grayscale before Bitmap
steps.text: For Bitmap, choose Image > Mode > Grayscale first. Then go back to Image > Mode and click Bitmap. Bitmap only works after the file is in Grayscale.

steps.name: Read the warning and click OK
steps.text: If Photoshop warns that converting will flatten layers, discard channels, or reduce color information, read it before you click. Button labels can change between versions, so read the dialog on your screen.

steps.name: Check the result
steps.text: Open Image > Mode again and confirm the mode you chose is now set. Compare skin tones, logos, and brand colors with your RGB copy. Press ⌘Z to undo if anything looks wrong.

steps.name: If the Mode menu is greyed out
steps.text: Go to Image > Mode and choose 8 Bits/Channel if the file is at 32 Bits/Channel. Then press Q to turn off Quick Mask and try the mode again.

shortcuts.action: Save As (keep a copy before converting)
Turn Quick Mask on or off

troubleshooting.fix: Check the bit depth under Image > Mode. If the file is at 32 Bits/Channel, choose 8 Bits/Channel, then try the mode again.

troubleshooting.problem: CMYK Color is missing from the list
troubleshooting.fix: Turn off Quick Mask. Press Q or click Quick Mask in the Tools panel. If a Quick Mask channel is still in the Channels panel, delete it.
Convert the file to Grayscale first with Image > Mode > Grayscale. Then choose Image > Mode > Bitmap.

troubleshooting.problem: Black artifacts or banding after RGB to CMYK
troubleshooting.fix: On Photoshop 27.8 or later on macOS Tahoe, turn off Use Graphics Processor under Photoshop > Settings > Performance, then convert again.

troubleshooting.problem: Canvas looks washed out after an update
troubleshooting.fix: Omnimend reports this bug in Photoshop 27.9.0 on Mac. Update to 27.9.1 or later, then reopen the file.

troubleshooting.problem: Colors look wrong after converting to CMYK
troubleshooting.fix: Compare against the RGB master, adjust in RGB, and convert again. Expect some shift, and check brand colors specifically.
